Check satisfiability

Source: R/solver.R
z3_check.Rd

Decides whether the assertions of a solver or optimizer, together with the optional assumptions, are satisfiable.

Usage

z3_check(x, ..., timeout = NULL)

Arguments

x

A z3_solver or z3_optimize.

...

Assumptions: Boolean expressions or lists of them.

timeout

NULL, or a time limit in milliseconds (a positive whole number) for this check only; see the Timeouts section.

Value

"sat", "unsat" or "unknown".

Details

The result is one of three strings:

  • "sat": a model exists; retrieve it with z3_model().

  • "unsat": no model exists; z3_unsat_core() explains why when assumptions or tracked assertions were used.

  • "unknown": Z3 gave up, for example because of a timeout, a resource limit, or a theory (such as nonlinear integer arithmetic or quantifiers) for which Z3 has no complete decision procedure. "unknown" is not "unsat"; see z3_reason_unknown().

Assumptions are Boolean expressions that hold for this check only. They are not added to the solver.

Timeouts

timeout limits this check to that many milliseconds, replacing any timeout of the solver or optimizer for this call only; a check that runs out of time returns "unknown". Afterwards z3r sets the object's parameters back, also when the check fails or is interrupted: the timeout set with z3_set_params() returns, and without one the object gets the context's timeout: the one set through z3r (z3_context(timeout = ) or z3_update_param()), or else a global timeout that was in force when the context was made, or none. Z3 cannot remove a parameter, so the object then keeps that value as its own: a later change of the context's timeout, or of a global timeout or solver.timeout set with z3_global_param_set(), no longer reaches it. Printing the object shows the parameters z3r has set on it.

Interrupting a check

While a check runs, Z3 installs its own handler for the interrupt signal (Z3's ctrl_c parameter, on by default). Pressing Ctrl-C (or the stop button of a front end that sends an interrupt signal) cancels the check and leaves the solver usable. For a z3_solver, z3r then raises an ordinary R interrupt, so tryCatch(..., interrupt = ) works as for any R computation. A z3_optimize reports the same reason ("canceled") for an interrupt, a timeout and a resource limit, so an interrupted optimizer check returns "unknown" instead. Front ends that do not send a signal (such as RGui on Windows) cannot interrupt Z3; set a timeout or rlimit with z3_set_params() there. R code running inside the check (a callback) can stop it with z3_interrupt().

Examples

ctx <- z3_context()
x <- z3_int(ctx, "x")
p <- z3_bool(ctx, "p")
s <- z3_solver(ctx)
z3_add(s, z3_implies(p, x > 10), x < 5)
z3_check(s)
#> [1] "sat"
z3_check(s, p)
#> [1] "unsat"
z3_unsat_core(s)
#> $p
#> <z3_expr Bool> p
#> 
z3_check(s, timeout = 5000)
#> [1] "sat"
